questions.learningObjective: Explain how division of labor on a moving line reshaped factory work.
questions.stem: Your design brief for a new appliance plant asks how moving work onto a moving conveyor will change the factory floor. Which effect best captures the core change?

options.text: Each worker performs one repetitive task on a moving line, and the line's pace sets the output for everyone.
Each worker builds a whole product from start to finish, so skill and variety grow at every station.
options.misconception: Belief that workers still build whole products.

options.text: A few master workers perform the hardest steps, and the rest of the line waits for them to finish.
options.misconception: Belief that only a few masters do the hardest steps.

options.text: Machines do most of the work, so the plant needs engineers and far fewer operators than before.
options.misconception: Belief that machines remove nearly all the jobs.

questions.explanation: Assembly-line work divides each product into small repetitive steps, and the moving line sets every station's pace. Believing workers would still build whole products ignores that division of labor.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a weighted site-comparison table for a plant siting decision.
questions.stem: A client brief lists three candidate sites for a new plant using four factors scored from 1 to 5: freight access, labor supply, power cost, and customer proximity. Town A scores 5-3-4-5, Town B scores 3-5-5-3, and Town C scores 4-4-2-4. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Town B must be chosen, because it posts the highest single score in two of the four factors.
options.misconception: Belief that the best single factor settles the choice.

options.text: Town A leads if freight and customer proximity matter most, while Town B wins if labor supply dominates.
Town C should be rejected outright, because its power cost score of 2 is the lowest in the table.
options.misconception: Belief that one weak factor disqualifies a balanced site.

options.text: The three towns are effectively tied, since each total falls between 16 and 18 points out of 20.
options.misconception: Belief that adding up scores makes sites interchangeable.

questions.explanation: A siting brief only favors a town once the designer states which factors weigh most, and Town A leads on the two that dominate freight-heavy work. One weak score does not disqualify a site.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the economic process that produced crowded tenement neighborhoods.
questions.stem: Your brief on worker housing for a factory district asks you to explain how rapid industrial hiring and low pay combined to produce crowded tenement neighborhoods. Write a short account of that process.

answer.exemplar: Tenements rose because employers hired large numbers of workers quickly while wages stayed low, so a family could afford only one or two rooms. Landlords subdivided old houses into windowless sleeping rooms with shared kitchens and toilets, and that crowding helped spread disease. Plague and tuberculosis outbreaks in the 1890s drew public attention and pushed cities toward tenement inspection and stricter building codes.

questions.explanation: Tenement overcrowding came from cheap factory wages meeting scarce housing, which pushed families into subdivided rooms. The brief asks for causation, not merely a description of crowded conditions.
questions.hint: Consider wages, arrivals, and what landlords could charge.

options.text: The law worked as intended, because suspending labor migration ended the wage competition workers complained about.

The law was unenforceable, because Congress could not restrict immigration by statute under the Constitution.
options.misconception: Belief that restricting immigration was unconstitutional.

questions.explanation: The law was defended as a response to wage pressure, yet restricting arrivals also narrowed the labor pool employers relied on. Calling it a jobs program, or constitutionally void, misreads how bans worked.
questions.hint: Ask what the law claimed and what employers then faced.

stimulus.body: The inspector recorded that loose waste cotton had been swept beneath the cutting machines on the eighth floor and that the sprinkler guard had not yet been installed. options.misconception: Belief that the missing guard made the fire unpredictable.

options.text: The report proves the fire began because the machines were new that year, and new machines were always unsafe.
options.misconception: Belief that machine age alone explains the disaster.

options.text: The report shows the survivors were at fault, since they never tested the stairways before the alarm sounded.
options.misconception: Belief that survivor behavior set the death toll.

options.text: The report links the fire to combustible waste under the machines and blocked stairs, both under management's control.

questions.explanation: The report names two management-controlled hazards, combustible waste and locked exit stairs, so the toll was not a matter of chance. Blaming machine age or survivor conduct ignores what the document records.

options.text: The bill is weaker than a single strict rule, because splitting safety into parts lets each plant satisfy only the easiest one.
options.misconception: Belief that dividing rules into parts makes them easier to dodge.

options.text: The bill links building design, housekeeping, and exit access, so it addresses hazards that interact rather than one isolated risk.
The bill mainly creates paperwork, because inspectors will record violations without changing how plants operate.

questions.explanation: Disasters often come from several ordinary hazards lining up, so ventilation, housekeeping, and exits must be checked together. One rule rarely covers everything, and split rules invite evasion.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how installment credit changed household spending and debt.
questions.stem: A retailer brief notes that a family can buy a radio on monthly installments without any cash down payment. Which consequence did installment credit most directly produce in 1920s consumer spending?

options.text: Durable goods became cheap enough that most families owned a radio within a year of its introduction.
options.misconception: Belief that installment credit made goods genuinely cheap.

options.text: Households avoided borrowing entirely, so installment plans kept consumer debt flat while sales rose.
options.misconception: Belief that installment buying left debt unchanged.

options.text: Households bought durable goods before saving the cash, so spending ran ahead of income and debt grew.
Rural families bought more goods than urban ones, because installment plans were offered mainly in farming districts.
options.misconception: Belief that installment credit spread mainly among rural families.

questions.explanation: Installment credit let households pay from future earnings, so purchases outran current income and debt climbed. Believing plans were debt-free, or that goods simply became cheap, misses the shift in who paid.

options.misconception: Belief that output growth alone settles questions of living standards.

options.text: Wages alone prove national prosperity, because the highest regional wage shows what most workers earned.
options.misconception: Belief that the best paid region represents most workers.

options.text: The south lagged only because its factories were newer, since new plants always pay lower starting wages.
options.misconception: Belief that low southern wages simply marked new plants.

options.text: National prosperity in the 1920s was uneven, because wage and production gains differed sharply by region.

questions.explanation: Wages from $19 to $34 and growth from 2 to 14 percent show gains concentrated in some regions rather than shared. Reading the best region as typical, or blaming plant age, misstates the unevenness.

answer.exemplar: Families accepted the arrangement because low industrial wages left them no larger housing budget, and landlords subdivided buildings faster than cities inspected them. questions.explanation: Tenement conditions endured because low wages and fast arrivals left families with no cheaper option and inspections lagged behind. The brief asks why the arrangement persisted, not merely what it looked like.

options.text: Because quotas were tied to census figures, they were unenforceable, since employers ignored them and workers kept entering.

options.text: Because quotas were tied to census figures, they cut arrivals from every country to the same small number each year.

options.text: Because quotas were tied to census figures, they pushed most new arrivals into cities with strong ethnic institutions.

questions.explanation: Census-based quotas capped the national origins of arrivals and sharpened the ethnic mix of the immigrant stream. Believing they cut every group equally, or pushed arrivals toward cities, misreads the mechanism.

questions.learningObjective: Draw an inference about fire severity from a response timeline.

stimulus.body: The first alarm was sounded at 10:25 in the morning. options.misconception: Belief that the outcome proves the responders deliberately delayed.

options.text: The delay in controlling the upper floors points to building design that spread fire upward, not merely to slow arrival.
The log shows the alarm was raised too late, since the working day meant workers were inside for an unusual number of hours.
options.misconception: Belief that the late alarm reflects unusual working hours.

options.text: The log indicates the building was structurally sound, because a sound building would not have needed standpipe water.
options.misconception: Belief that needing standpipe water proves structural soundness.

questions.explanation: Water reached the upper floors only after a delay, pointing to vertical spread through stairs and shafts. Blaming the responders, a late alarm, or structural soundness exceeds what the log records.

questions.stem: Your brief proposes a state inspection regime covering ventilation, machine guarding, and fire exits, with fines set by the size of the plant. Synthesize what the penalty design adds to the inspection itself.

options.misconception: Belief that inspectors physically remove all hazards.

options.text: Fines scaled to plant size punish small workshops unfairly, because they have less profit to give up.
options.misconception: Belief that size based fines are unfair to small firms.

options.text: Fines scaled to plant size make violations cost more where the risk is greatest, linking enforcement to ability to pay.
Fines scaled to plant size discourage inspectors, since small sums on small plants attract little attention.
options.misconception: Belief that modest fines cause inspectors to neglect violations.

questions.explanation: A fine a large firm absorbs trivially changes nothing, so scaled penalties pressure firms with the most at stake. Calling such fines unfair, unnecessary, or self-defeating misses how deterrence works.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why reformers chose building codes rather than public housing.
questions.stem: A community brief asks you to explain why reformers in the 1890s pressed for stricter tenement rules instead of trying to build public housing. Write a short account of that choice.

answer.exemplar: Reformers focused on codes because the failures they described were specific and fixable: dark rooms, exit doors that opened inward, defective plumbing, and courtyards used as trash pits. Each could be addressed by inspection and minimum standards enforced against landlords, which seemed far more achievable than constructing housing at public expense. Codes could also reassure middle-class voters that the city was protecting families without committing to a costly housing program.

questions.explanation: Reformers chose codes because the hazards they saw were concrete and could be policed through inspection, while public housing demanded a new public program. The brief asks why one remedy gained ground.
questions.hint: Consider what an inspector could measure on a routine visit.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how informal separation of immigrant districts hardened into law.
questions.stem: A landlord's brief asks you to explain why cities in the late nineteenth century often separated immigrant districts from other neighborhoods by law as well as by custom. Write a short account of that process.

answer.exemplar: Legal separation grew out of the same fears that shaped the tenement: established residents worried about falling property values, cheaper labor, and crowded schools if new immigrant families moved in. Zoning rules and separate school districts turned those fears into formal boundaries, and agents could then direct buyers toward particular streets. Over time the legal boundary hardened a pattern custom had only partly created, and the districts stayed poor long after the first families had moved on.

questions.explanation: Districts became legally walled off because property owners and schools wanted protection from rapid demographic change, turning custom into code. The brief asks how informal separation hardened into formal law.
questions.hint: Consider who wanted these boundaries and what they gained.

questions.stem: A brief for a new building type asks you to explain why reformers argued that better housing should be built near transit lines rather than in the outer districts where land was cheap. Write a short account of that argument.

answer.exemplar: Reformers favored sites near transit because location shaped daily life: a worker in a distant suburb spent a large share of the day riding to and from work, leaving less time for family, rest, and community. Transit access also lowered the cost of reaching shops, schools, and clinics, and kept families near the jobs and social networks that made settlement possible for newcomers. Cheap outlying land could house people, but it did not replace the connections that made urban life workable.

questions.explanation: Transit access determined how much of a worker's day and money went to travel, so reformers treated location as part of housing quality. The brief asks why siting mattered, not what buildings looked like.
questions.hint: Consider what distance cost a worker in time and money each day.

options.text: The line is only as good as its upstream planning, since a defect or shortage at one station stops every station behind it.
The claim is correct, because inspection mattered only in the era before conveyors were introduced.
options.misconception: Belief that inspection was obsolete once conveyors appeared.

options.text: The claim is partly right, since only a first station ever encounters a shortage of material.
options.misconception: Belief that shortages stop only the first station.

questions.explanation: Each station depends on the one before it, so planning and inspection protect the whole line, not one step. Believing specialists remove coordination, or that only the first station feels shortages, misreads the design.
questions.hint: Ask what a shortage at one station does to the stations behind it.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate landed cost to compare warehouse sites.
questions.stem: A brief for a distribution warehouse lists distances from the main port: site one 5 miles, site two 60 miles, site three 25 miles, and notes the port charged $40 per ton at the wharf plus $9 per mile of drayage. Which site does this cost rule favor?

options.text: Site two, because a larger site always receives a lower per ton wharf rate from the port.
options.misconception: Belief that larger sites get lower wharf rates.

options.text: Site three, since 25 miles is short enough to make the difference between the three sites negligible.
options.misconception: Belief that the difference in drayage distance is negligible.

options.text: Site one, since its drayage cost of $45 per ton adds to a $40 wharf charge and beats the others on landed cost.
No site can be ranked, because the brief omits the cost of moving goods from the port to the customer.
options.misconception: Belief that landed cost needs customer freight costs.

questions.explanation: Landed cost is wharf charge plus drayage, so site one at $45 a ton beats site three at $265 and site two at $580 on this rule. Assuming the gap is negligible misreads the data.
questions.hint: Add the wharf charge to the drayage cost for each site.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why early tenement codes focused on light, air, and exits.
questions.stem: A brief asks you to explain why tenement reform in many cities began with rules about light, air, and exits rather than with limits on how many people could sleep in a room. Write a short account of that reasoning.

answer.exemplar: Light, air, and exit rules were easier to define and to enforce than occupancy limits. An inspector could stand in a corridor and see whether windows opened, whether hallways were clear, and whether doors opened outward, while counting sleepers in a dark room required a nightly census that no inspector could keep. Because these measures were measurable at a glance, cities could adopt them early and still claim they were protecting tenants from the deadliest dangers of crowding.

questions.explanation: Reformers began with light, air, and exits because those were visible during an inspection, while sleeping density needed constant monitoring. The brief asks why the earlier rules were chosen.
questions.hint: Think about what an inspector could check in a short visit.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Trace the immediate labor-market effect of a numerical immigration ceiling.
questions.stem: A brief asks what immediate effect a numerical ceiling on immigration is most likely to have produced in the labor market of a receiving city. Which answer is best?

options.text: Housing demand vanished, since most new residents of these cities arrived as settled families, not as workers.
options.misconception: Belief that immigrants arrived mainly as settled families.

options.text: Employers received an unlimited supply of new workers, since a ceiling set only the total and never the sources.
options.misconception: Belief that a ceiling guarantees abundant labor.

options.text: Wages fell immediately, because employers passed every saved wage cost on to their customers.
options.misconception: Belief that a supply cut translates straight into falling wages.

options.text: Employers in the fastest growing trades had fewer new arrivals to hire, tightening competition for those remaining.

questions.explanation: A ceiling reduces the number of new workers available, so expanding trades compete more sharply for those already present. Believing a ceiling guarantees abundant labor, or that wages fall at once, misreads it.
questions.hint: Ask who competes for the workers who are already there.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Draw a conclusion about management decisions from an uninsured safety measure.
questions.stem: A brief asks which conclusion can be drawn from the fact that a garment plant's owners had not installed the fire alarm their insurer had specified. Which reading is best?

options.text: The owners were powerless to follow the insurer's advice, since the law barred private inspection of workplaces entirely.
options.misconception: Belief that the law prohibited private inspection of workplaces.

options.text: The owners chose to keep operating without a specified protection, which bears on how the outcome was shaped.
The alarm would have been useless, because detectors of that era could not sound a factory floor.
options.misconception: Belief that alarm technology of the period was ineffective.

options.text: The insurer intended to cancel the policy, which shows the company sought to shut the plant down.
options.misconception: Belief that the insurer wanted to close the plant.

questions.explanation: A specified alarm never installed shows a decision to operate without a recommended protection, relevant to how the outcome unfolded. Believing the law blocked advice or that alarms were useless misreads it.
questions.hint: Ask what the missing alarm tells you about the owners' choices.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Argue the case for unannounced inspection of workplaces.
questions.stem: A proposal in your brief would require factories to be inspected without warning, and you must weigh the case for it. Which argument most strongly supports the proposal?

options.text: Unannounced inspection is best because it shortens each visit, allowing more plants to be checked each year.
options.misconception: Belief that surprise visits take less inspector time.

options.text: Unannounced inspection is best because it removes inspectors from contact with management entirely.
options.misconception: Belief that surprise visits require avoiding management contact.

options.text: Unannounced inspection is the only way to observe conditions on an ordinary working day, since announced visits can be prepared for.
Unannounced inspection is best because it guarantees that every violation found leads to a fine.
options.misconception: Belief that surprise visits ensure every violation is fined.

questions.explanation: The strongest argument concerns what observers see, since a plant can look different for a prepared visit than on a normal shift. Believing surprise visits reduce contact or guarantee fines misreads the point.
questions.hint: Ask what a plant looks like on a day nobody expects a visit.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret installment balances and delinquency data by income level.
questions.stem: A brief on household credit lists installment balances in 1927 at $600 for households above $5,000 in annual income and $150 for households below $2,000, with delinquencies concentrated in the lower group. Which reading is best supported?

options.text: Balances of $150 and $600 show that repayment risk was evenly distributed across income levels.
options.misconception: Belief that the data shows risk spread evenly across incomes.

options.text: Credit stayed confined to the wealthiest households, since only they held large installment balances.
options.misconception: Belief that installment credit was used only by the rich.

options.text: The lower group's delinquencies prove that lenders deliberately targeted families they knew would default.
options.misconception: Belief that lenders aimed to extend credit to families expected to fail.

options.text: Credit reached down the income scale while repayment risk stayed concentrated where incomes were irregular and thin.

questions.explanation: A $150 balance among lower income households shows credit reaching down the income scale, while delinquencies there point to irregular earnings. Believing credit stayed with the rich misreads the data.
questions.hint: Ask what a balance of $150 in a poor household signifies.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Combine building and wage evidence to describe the distribution of prosperity.
questions.stem: A final brief asks you to combine a builder's account of 1920s housing starts with a union's account of mill wages, and to explain what together they say about the distribution of prosperity. Which reading is best?

options.text: Private construction expanded, and expanding construction always raises the wages of nearby factory workers.
options.misconception: Belief that a construction boom necessarily lifts factory wages.

options.text: Private construction expanded while industrial pay stayed flat, so the visible boom in building sat beside stagnation for wage earners.
Industrial pay stayed flat, which shows the decade produced no economic growth of any kind anywhere.
options.misconception: Belief that flat factory wages mean no growth occurred anywhere.

options.text: The two accounts cannot be compared, because a builder's starts and a union's wage figures measure entirely different things.
options.misconception: Belief that housing starts and wages can never share a frame.

questions.explanation: Side by side the accounts show construction expanding while wage earners' pay did not, which is what uneven prosperity looks like. Believing construction lifts factory wages, or flat pay means no growth, misreads it.
questions.hint: Ask what a worker and a builder each experienced in the same decade.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the production logic behind interchangeable parts.
questions.stem: A brief for a parts maker asks which production arrangement best matches the logic of mass production with interchangeable parts. Which arrangement fits?

options.text: Every part produced on its own machine, so the separate origins of the machines guarantee that parts will fit.
options.misconception: Belief that different machines alone ensure parts will fit.

options.text: Every part finished by hand to fit the first unit, so each product is unique and needs no standard.
options.misconception: Belief that unique hand finished parts mark interchangeable production.

options.text: Every part made to the same written specification, so any unit can be assembled with any other off the line.
Every part stored in one warehouse, so workers carry a single part type to the line each morning.
options.misconception: Belief that storing one part type makes parts interchangeable.

questions.explanation: Interchangeability depends on a specification held to across every part, letting any unit be assembled with any other. Believing uniqueness or single part storage produces it misreads the requirement.
questions.hint: Ask what must be true of two parts made weeks apart.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Assess the risks and benefits of locating a plant among immigrant labor.
questions.stem: A brief asks you to judge the practice of siting a plant in a town where the majority of workers had arrived from abroad. Which assessment is most balanced?

options.text: It was regulated by federal law, so a company's choice of labor source was never a local decision.
options.misconception: Belief that federal law fixed each employer's labor source.

options.text: It was purely advantageous, because hiring locally always strengthened a firm's relationship with its community.
options.misconception: Belief that hiring locally always deepened community ties.

options.text: It was unwise in every case, because foreign born workers never carried the skills a modern plant required.
options.misconception: Belief that immigrant workers never held needed skills.

options.text: It lowered transport costs and used available labor, but it also tied the firm to a group facing legal restriction.

questions.explanation: Local hiring cut transport costs and used nearby workers, while concentrating a firm on a group facing legal restriction. Believing it was purely advantageous, or that immigrants lacked skills, misses the risk.
questions.hint: Ask what exposure came with relying on that labor pool.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Weigh private landlord choice against public inaction in tenement overcrowding.
questions.stem: Your housing brief asks you to weigh a claim that tenement overcrowding was mainly a matter of private landlord choice, since the city never forced anyone to subdivide. Which assessment is best?

options.text: The claim is correct, because landlords were free to act and no public pressure ever touched the housing market.
options.misconception: Belief that no public pressure affected housing decisions.

options.text: The claim is too narrow, because rising rents and rapid arrival made subdivision profitable while public housing was not built.
The claim is correct, because workers could always have moved to the suburbs if their rooms were too small.
options.misconception: Belief that moving to suburbs was an easy alternative.

options.text: The claim is correct, because overcrowding could only be measured properly after the housing reforms of the 1900s.
options.misconception: Belief that housing conditions could not be judged earlier.

questions.explanation: Landlords subdivided because tenants needed rooms and cities built no alternatives, so the outcome owed as much to what government did not do as to private choice. Believing nobody pressed for reform ignores the shortage.
questions.hint: Ask what families could have moved to instead.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a slower inflow from a shrinking immigrant population.
questions.stem: A brief asks you to evaluate a claim that immigration restriction produced a lasting decline in the foreign born population of a northern industrial city. Which evaluation is most defensible?

options.text: The claim is sound, because foreign born residents of that city all left within a decade of the restriction.
options.misconception: Belief that existing immigrant residents left en masse.

options.text: The claim is sound, because every year of restricted entry lowers the total number of residents in the city.
options.misconception: Belief that a smaller inflow must reduce the population.

options.text: The claim confuses arrivals with population, since a lower inflow reduces growth while residents already there persist.
The claim is sound, because the city's total population fell during the same years the inflow was restricted.
options.misconception: Belief that restricting inflow reduced the city population.

questions.explanation: A smaller inflow slows population growth rather than shrinking a population that already lives there. Believing lower arrivals reduce total residents mistakes growth rate for size.
questions.hint: Ask whether a smaller flow of newcomers shrinks or slows a population.
